The first node, in the accent color, collects the most links in every panel (degree 6, 5, and 7), showing how early, well-connected nodes become hubs." width="100%"} Grows a graph by adding nodes one at a time, with each new node connecting to `m` existing nodes with probability proportional to degree. This creates scale-free networks with power-law degree distributions. Growth starts from a complete graph on the first `m + 1` nodes. Each later node then picks `m` distinct targets among the nodes generated so far, weighting each candidate by its current degree, so well-connected nodes keep attracting new links ("the rich get richer"). The result has `n` nodes and `m(m + 1) / 2 + (n - m - 1) * m` edges, every node has degree at least `m`, and the oldest nodes tend to become hubs. In a directed graph each attachment edge points from the newer node to the older one it attaches to. The `n` new nodes are unlabelled and get the next available node IDs. Existing nodes are left untouched: they are neither connected to nor counted when choosing attachment targets. Preferential attachment graphs are a standard model for networks dominated by a few hubs, such as: - citation networks, the web's link graph, and some social networks - null models with a heavy-tailed degree distribution, to contrast with `add_gnp_graph()` or `add_gnm_graph()` - testing how algorithms (or attacks and failures) behave when degree is very unequal ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [n]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Total number of nodes to add, including the initial `m + 1` seed clique. Must be greater than `m=`. [m]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[2]{.dv}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Number of edges each new node attaches with (default `2`). Larger values give a denser graph with an average degree close to `2 * m`. Must be at least `1` and less than `n=`; `m=1` grows a tree. [seed]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Optional[int]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Integer seed for the random number generator. The same `seed=` with the same `n=` and `m=` always gives the same graph. If `None` (default), the result differs on every call. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Self for method chaining. The graph is modified in place. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `m=` is less than `1` or not less than `n=`. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} Each new node attaches to `m` existing nodes chosen with probability proportional to their current degree, so already well-connected nodes tend to accumulate even more connections. This "rich get richer" dynamic is what produces the scale-free, power-law degree distribution the Barabási-Albert model is known for. The edge count is fixed by `n` and `m`: `6` edges in the starting clique plus `3` for each of the remaining `96` nodes gives `294`: ::: {#f6b999bc .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ( ec.Graph() .add_pa_graph(n=100, m=3, seed=23) ) graph.count_nodes(), graph.count_edges() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (100, 294) ``` ::: ::: The degree sequence is very uneven: a few hubs collect dozens of links, while the many late arrivals keep the minimum degree of `m=3`: ::: {#663079af .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} degrees = sorted( (graph.get_degree(nid) for nid in graph.get_node_ids(limit=None)), reverse=True ) degrees[:5], degrees[-5:] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` ([30, 29, 23, 18, 13], [3, 3, 3, 3, 3]) ``` ::: ::: Compared with a uniform random graph of the same size (built with `add_gnm_graph()`), the largest degrees are far higher, which is the signature of preferential attachment: ::: {#d8b48c7f .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} pa = ec.Graph().add_pa_graph(n=500, m=2, seed=23) uniform = ec.Graph().add_gnm_graph(n=500, m=pa.count_edges(), seed=23) def top_degrees(g): degrees = [g.get_degree(nid) for nid in g.get_node_ids(limit=None)] return sorted(degrees, reverse=True)[:5] top_degrees(pa), top_degrees(uniform) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` ([35, 33, 30, 30, 26], [10, 10, 10, 9, 9]) ``` ::: ::: With `m=1` each new node adds a single edge, so the result is a tree. In a directed graph the attachment edges point from the newcomer to the node it attached to; only the first edge, `1->2`, belongs to the two-node starting clique and runs from older to newer: ::: {#e9062296 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} tree = ec.Graph(directed=True).add_pa_graph(n=6, m=1, seed=23) tree.get_edges_str_repr() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` ['1->2', '3->2', '4->3', '5->3', '6->2'] ``` ::: :::
